svadhisthana:5-3-8.heading: A proper craft and an honest harvest
paragraphs: Your pleasure might begin with signing up for a workshop. In Svadhisthana, the Hierophant shapes the form your interests take: you like learning from someone who knows the craft — the basics, the techniques and an order of things laid down long before you arrived. The Empress feeds the desire: you are drawn to whatever grows and bears fruit, when a shapeless lump suddenly turns into something you can actually use. And Justice measures out the feeling afterwards: the joy is complete when the result matches the work you put in.

Say you are learning to throw pots. The first weeks are centring, walls, more centring, just as the teacher says. Then one day a cup rises out of the clay, and you want to make ten more — for friends, for home, as presents. **A skill learned honestly gives you the sweetest fruit.** The cup is not a lucky accident but a result you earned, and your morning coffee tastes especially good from it.

It gets harder when the scales don’t balance. You have been going to classes for three months and your walls are still crooked, while the person at the next wheel is already firing a whole tea set. You want to know where the mistake lies: in you, in the clay, in the teacher’s method. A pastime meant for pleasure turns into an exam, where every failed pot feels like an unfair mark. If enjoyment is only handed out after an inspection, an evening at the workshop starts to feel more like a shift than a rest.

svadhisthana:5-6-11.heading: Passion inside a beautiful form
paragraphs: You enjoy pleasures that have a shape of their own. The Hierophant shows in the pastimes you choose: a school, an etiquette, levels of mastery do not get in the way — they keep the joy flowing between its banks. The Lovers spark the desire: your interest flares up next to another person, when two people are open to each other and move as one. And Strength governs what stays with you afterwards: you hold a strong feeling gently, the way the woman on the card holds the lion — neither crushing it nor letting it tear everything apart.

Take an evening of Argentine tango. An invitation with a glance across the room, three dances in a row with the same partner, the rule of not chatting while the music plays — for you these conventions are like the banks of a river. Within them you can allow yourself a great deal: closeness, trust, play. **Passion sounds brighter for you when it has a clear form.** You come home with flushed cheeks, but with no chaos inside.

The difficulty is that the form can start making decisions for you. If the evening doesn’t work out — nobody asked you to dance, your partner seemed distracted — you smile as etiquette requires and gently smother the hurt. Restraint keeps you from spoiling the occasion, but the frustration builds up: it goes unspoken, the desire goes unnamed, and the next evening begins with caution. One day you may notice that you have carefully tamed not just the hurt but the desire itself — and the dance you came for never happened.

svadhisthana:5-21-8.heading: Working through the course, cover to cover
paragraphs: For you, pleasure can look like a syllabus. The Hierophant sets the method: you enjoy studying within a recognised system — a course, a textbook, levels, a teacher who leads you from the simple to the complex. The World supplies the motive: you are drawn to completeness, to the moment when scattered rules come together into a single picture and you can see the whole subject at once. Justice speaks in the feeling afterwards: the joy is real when the assessment is honest and the result is in proportion to the effort.

Say you are learning Italian. Verbs, prepositions and hundreds of exercises are dull on their own, but you know where they lead. And one day you watch an Italian film without subtitles and laugh in the right place: the rules have suddenly become living speech. **The best pleasure is to see the subject whole and know that every step towards it was taken honestly.** A certificate on the wall is nice, but nicer still is the sense that every line on it was earned.

The flip side is joy postponed until the finish. Until the course is completed and the exam is passed, the pleasure somehow doesn’t count. Dropping out halfway feels like failure, even if the six months were interesting. And a hobby with no levels or marks is unsettling: how do you know you are doing it right? Then learning turns into a record of grades, with almost no room left for the simple pleasure of understanding the language now, halfway along the road.

svadhisthana:8-3-11.heading: Ten ideas and one free evening
paragraphs: You may have more ideas than evenings. The Empress gives birth to them: desire spreads like a garden — you want to make things, bake, paint, plant up the windowsill, and every idea promises fruit. Justice sets the way this abundance enters your life: you measure out time for pleasure honestly, without taking it from your duties or the people close to you. What remains afterwards is the feeling of Strength: you don’t stifle the urge to drop everything for a new project — you hold it back gently, and it doesn’t fade.

On Friday you feel like starting three things at once: a shelf from old floorboards, a new song on the guitar and a photo walk around town. You pick one, give it Saturday morning, and give the others their own time during the week. **Abundance does not turn into chaos for you: every desire gets its share, and none of them is smothered.** The other ideas ripen patiently, like a crop in the vegetable patch — their turn will come.

But a fair queue sometimes stretches on for too long. Strength holds back gently, and that is convenient: desire doesn’t make a scene, it agrees to wait. Chores, loved ones and urgent requests always find a reason to take its share, and once again you fairly step aside. Ideas pile up in your notes, the boards gather dust in the shed, and the Empress is left without a harvest. An urge that has been gently tamed so many times one day simply stops coming — the evening is free, but there is nothing left to want.

svadhisthana:8-6-14.heading: Shared joy, split down the middle
paragraphs: Your liveliest desires may be born next to another person. That is the Lovers: you are drawn to wherever joy can be shared with someone dear to you, where the two of you can be open with each other. Justice determines how these pleasures work in practice: fairly, in turn, with both people’s tastes taken into account. The aftertaste comes from Temperance: different wants blend like water poured between the angel’s two cups, leaving a soft, even contentment.

This Friday you choose the film; next Friday your partner does. In summer you go where they are keen to go, and in autumn wherever you feel drawn. Their love of noisy gatherings and your longing for quiet are not at war: the evening starts at a friend’s place and ends with just the two of you in the kitchen. **Shared joy tastes better to you than a solo one — as long as both people are fairly counted in.** Nobody walks away feeling sacrificed, and so you want to do it again and again.

The trouble begins when the score matters more than the desire. “It’s my turn tonight” — and you end up choosing not what you want but what the rota says. Temperance smooths the sharp corners, and gradually every evening becomes a compromise in which nobody gets what they really, strongly wanted. There are no rows, fairness is observed, the aftertaste is even — but not a single Saturday sticks in the memory, because the bright things never made it onto the shared list.

svadhisthana:8-9-17.heading: Refine it in silence, then give it away
paragraphs: The Hermit with his lantern explains where your interest in Svadhisthana comes from: a solitary search, when you can go deep into a subject and work it out for yourself. Justice shows how that interest takes shape: you enjoy work where precision matters and every word or detail has been weighed. And the Star arrives at the end: the best feeling comes when what you found has been handed to others and carries hope and light for someone else.

For example, you are translating a favourite book that no one has translated yet. In the evenings, in silence, you weigh every sentence, check the meaning, rewrite a paragraph for the fifth time — and it isn’t torture but pleasure. Then you post the translation for anyone to read, and a stranger writes that they had been waiting for it for years. **Your joy is to make something precisely and alone, and then generously pass on its light.** The Hermit’s lantern does not shine for him alone.

The hardest part turns out to be the handover. Carefully weighed work wants to become flawless, and solitude never hurries you: you can check once more, correct once more. The Star’s hope gets postponed until “when it’s ready”, and drafts pile up in a drawer. Until the piece reaches people, it lacks the very light it was all for — and the pleasure of precision slowly gives way to weariness from endless checking that nobody but you ever sees.

svadhisthana:8-12-20.heading: A puzzle that suddenly opens up
paragraphs: What really draws you in? Most likely a problem you can get stuck on. Justice shapes your leisure: you like games and pastimes with exact rules, where everything is fair and can be checked — chess, detective board games, tricky puzzles. The Hanged Man explains the pull: your interest is fuelled by the very state of being stuck, when the usual move doesn’t work and you have to look at things from the other side. And Judgement sounds in the feeling afterwards — like an awakening, when suddenly everything falls into place.

Say a chess study has resisted you for three evenings. You put the board aside, turn it round in your mind, look through your opponent’s eyes — and at some point you see the move that was in front of you all along. **The sweetest thing is the moment when what was stuck suddenly opens up and can be seen whole.** That feeling beats any win: as if you had woken up and seen the board anew. For its sake, no long pause or failed attempt feels wasted.

It’s harder with games that never opened up. Justice and Judgement together can easily turn play into a trial: you take a loss as a verdict and replay your mistakes until late at night. A move made at random brings no joy either — the win feels undeserved. The suspense that once drew you in grows heavy when no breakthrough comes. And your free time gradually becomes a court session, where you are both the prosecutor and the one passing sentence.

svadhisthana:8-21-11.heading: The wide world, with a clear plan
paragraphs: The wide world calls to you. Here the World sets the desire: your interest is born of fullness — seeing a country in its entirety, walking a route from start to finish, fitting the sea, the mountains and an old town into one trip. Justice decides how you make it happen: the holiday is well weighed, the budget fairly divided, each day given its own measure. And Strength lives in the feeling: you neither chase away your nerves before the unknown nor give in to them — you gently tame them, and they turn into courage.

Here you are, stepping off a train in a city where you know neither the language nor the streets. For some this is a reason to panic, but you have a plan and a calm “we’ll figure it out”. Within an hour you’ve found the market, by evening a viewpoint above the rooftops. **You enter the wide world with a clear plan and calm courage — and so it opens up to you whole.** The trip comes together as a complete story, one you enjoy remembering in order, day by day.

But planning and a hunger for completeness can squeeze pleasure into a timetable. The route has to pay off: see everything, miss nothing, fairly allocate every hour. And the sudden urge — to turn down a side street, to stay one more day where it feels good — Strength habitually holds back, because it’s not in the plan. You come home with a full list of sights, but the most alive part stayed round the corner you didn’t allow yourself to turn.

svadhisthana:11-3-14.heading: What grows in your hands without force
paragraphs: In Svadhisthana, joy for you is bound up with things that live and grow. The Empress is the source of desire: you are drawn to whatever ripens and bears fruit, be it a sourdough starter, seedlings on the windowsill or a garden. Strength shows in your hands: you don’t rush living things or break them, you guide them carefully, without force — the way the woman on the card calms the lion. And the feeling afterwards comes from Temperance: a quiet contentment in which patience and delight are mixed together.

Sourdough bread is a good example. You can’t force a starter; you can only feed it, wait and get a feel for it. You mix flour and water, fold the dough every half hour and watch it come alive. **You take pleasure in what grows in your hands without hurry or pressure.** In the morning there is a crusty loaf on the table, as if from the Empress’s own field of ripening wheat, and inside you an even, warm feeling: it all happened by itself, yet thanks to you.

The difficulty grows along with the abundance. The starter needs feeding, the seedlings need watering, the guests need a pie, and care quietly becomes an obligation. You handle living things so gently and keep your own impulses so even that there is no room left for sudden, spontaneous pleasure: lazing about for a day or dashing off on an unplanned trip feels out of place. The joy stays soft and dependable, but there are fewer and fewer sparks in it — and sometimes you wish someone would take care of you.

svadhisthana:11-6-17.heading: Courage with someone to give it to
paragraphs: Going on stage, singing at a friend’s wedding, showing your drawings — for many people this is frightening. Strength makes such acts possible: you don’t hide your nerves or let them knock you over, you gently lead them along. But it switches on when there is someone to do it for — that is how the Lovers work in Svadhisthana: you want to bring joy to the people you are drawn to and open with. And afterwards comes the Star: the light you gave returns as hope and warmth.

Imagine a close friend’s birthday. You have spent a month learning a song on the guitar, and you bring it out halfway through the evening. Your fingers tremble a little, but you look at your friend and play to the end. **Courage comes to you when there is someone to try for.** Afterwards everyone hugs, someone asks for an encore, and inside you it is quiet and bright, as if you had given something away and grown richer for it.

The weak spot is a joy that only switches on with an audience. When there is no one to please, the guitar stands in the corner: playing for yourself seems pointless, and a desire with no one to receive it quickly fades. The Star’s hope starts to depend on other people’s eyes. If a gift is met absent-mindedly, you gently hide your disappointment, smile and start preparing the next surprise. So the pleasure passes entirely to others, and you are left with courage alone — without a quiet joy in the activity itself.

svadhisthana:11-9-20.heading: Years of quiet and one living note
paragraphs: Some pleasures take years to ripen. The Hermit explains what draws you to them: your interest grows in solitude, when you can go deeper along your own path, by the light of your own lantern. Strength shows in the way you practise: without lurches or forcing yourself, gently coming back to the hard passage again and again. And the strongest feeling is brought by Judgement — the moment when long effort suddenly answers back, as if a trumpet had sounded inside you.

Say you are learning the cello. For months the sound scrapes, the studies won’t come, and nobody hears your evening practice. Then on some ordinary Tuesday a piece suddenly sounds — not perfect, but alive, and for the first time you hear music in it rather than notes. **Your pleasure ripens slowly and in silence, and arrives like an awakening.** Moments like this make you want to keep going, and every earlier evening takes on meaning.

Moments of awakening are rare, though, and evenings without them are many. Gentle persistence lets you endure for a long time — sometimes longer than you should. Ordinary practice starts to feel like preparation, where it is too early to be happy and there is nothing yet to show. The Hermit is in no hurry to go out to people, and the years pass in a quiet where neither a teacher nor a friend can tell you that you already sound good. While you wait for the breakthrough, the process itself slowly turns into a duty.

svadhisthana:11-12-5.heading: A tea pause done properly
paragraphs: In Svadhisthana, your interest is fuelled by the Hanged Man: you are drawn to pastimes where time seems suspended and you can sink in so deeply that your view of the world shifts. Strength sets the manner: you calm fuss and impatience gently, your hands grow steady and your movements precise. When it is all over, you are left with the feeling of the Hierophant — belonging to a tradition: it is good to know that people did this long before you and that this calm has a form of its own.

Take a tea ceremony. You warm the teaware, measure out the leaves, wait for the water to reach the right temperature — and don’t rush a single step. The fifth infusion opens up differently from the first, and you notice, because you are in no hurry. **You are filled by a pause that has its own form and its own ritual.** After an hour like that the world looks a little different, and inside it is calm, as if you had briefly stepped into a long tradition shared by many people.

Over time, the joy may start to demand the right setting. Without the right teaware, quiet and a free hour, pleasure somehow doesn’t seem allowed, and it’s easier to skip it altogether. Friends invite you to a noisy café, and you feel out of place: “that’s not how tea is drunk”. Strength gently holds back your irritation, but anything spontaneous begins to feel wrong. The pause that used to fill you turns into a ritual you can’t relax without — and the stopping itself becomes an obligation.

svadhisthana:11-15-8.heading: A tamed pull and honest scales
paragraphs: When something draws you in, it draws you in hard. The Devil kindles a thrill that grabs at once and lets go reluctantly: one more round, one more level, one more thing in the basket. But it is Strength that acts in you: you don’t cut the pull off with a ban, you tame it — gently and confidently, the way you would tame a powerful animal. And Justice can be heard in the feeling afterwards: you check the evening against honest scales — was time taken from your work and the people close to you?

Say it’s an online game with friends in the evenings. You don’t delete it in a fit of resolve, and you don’t vanish into it all night either. You make a deal with yourself: two matches once your tasks are done, more on Saturday. **You don’t fight your pull, you tame it — and that is why you can afford to indulge it.** The thrill is still a thrill, but it doesn’t give the orders, and after the game you feel calm: the scales balanced, and nobody was short-changed.

The fragile part is the endless negotiation. Taming easily turns into bargaining — “just one more, today’s allowed” — and gentleness quietly becomes giving in. The Devil’s chain is thinner than it looks. And if you slip and stay up half the night, Justice presents the bill: no games tomorrow, none the day after either. Pleasure becomes alternately earned and confiscated, and your evenings go not on joy but on deals with yourself and stern reckonings.

svadhisthana:11-21-5.heading: A great road laid down before you
paragraphs: Walking makes you happy. Your pull comes from the World, the dancing figure in the wreath: the fullness and breadth of life call you onto the road, into movement, into the feeling of being part of something whole. Strength shows in what you do: tiredness, rain or a ruined schedule you meet not with a lunge or a complaint but with calm endurance. And the Hierophant speaks in your feelings: what moves you most deeply is a path with a history and a tradition, one that thousands have walked before you.

Take an old pilgrim route — a week on foot from one small town to the next. In the morning you set out before dawn, during the day people from different countries overtake you and fall behind, and in the evening another stamp appears in your pilgrim’s passport. Your feet ache, but a rare feeling rises inside: you are walking where others walked before, and the world around you comes together as one. **It makes you happy to walk a great road laid down long before you.**

The danger lies in the words “the proper way”. If the path is valued for its tradition, then a shortened version somehow doesn’t count: taking a bus for part of the way feels like cheating, and a walk with no route and no stamps feels empty. Strength helps you endure a lot, and you push on where it would be time to stop, just to do it by the rules. Joy starts to depend on whether the experience gets counted, and the living breadth of the world narrows to a single path that was once declared correct.

svadhisthana:14-12-8.heading: Mix the colour, then let it dry
paragraphs: Your favourite things are processes that can’t be hurried. Temperance sets your way of doing things: you like to blend and combine — paint with water, flavours, sounds — pouring a little at a time from one cup into the other until you get exactly the shade you want. The Hanged Man feeds the desire: your interest grows in the pause, when everything goes still and you can look at the work differently. Then Justice sums up: after the work you are left with a sober, honest view of what you’ve done — what worked and what didn’t.

Watercolour is an almost perfect example. You mix a colour, lay down a wash — and wait: until the paper dries, there is nothing to be done. You can turn it upside down to see the composition afresh, the way the Hanged Man sees the world. **Here hurry gets you nowhere, and the pause does half the work — and that is exactly what draws you in.** In the evening you tell yourself honestly: the sky worked, the trees not yet — and this doesn’t upset you, it calls you on to the next sheet.

The difficulty lies in a pause that goes on too long and scales that are too precise. Each sheet is judged impartially, and you see its flaws more clearly than anyone. So as not to upset the balance you have found, you want to wait a little more, think a little more — and the bold brushstroke that could have brought the whole piece to life never gets made. The paintings come out neat but cautious, and the pleasure of mixing gives way to endless weighing: is it even worth starting?

svadhisthana:14-15-11.heading: A pull you water down yourself
paragraphs: Some hobbies are less about doing than about having. In Svadhisthana the Devil is a pull that hooks you and wants more: a new skein of yarn, one more brush, a rare record for the collection. Temperance shows how you live with it: you mix and alternate — a purchase with work from your stash, the new with the old — never letting one crowd out the other. And the feeling is held by Strength: when your hand reaches for the “buy” button, you know how to draw it gently back.

Take knitting. There’s enough yarn in the cupboard for two years, and the shop has a new batch of wool in an incredible colour. You buy one skein, not ten, and start a scarf with it, combining it with yarn that has long been waiting its turn. **You don’t put out a strong desire, you dilute it — and it becomes a source rather than a master.** In the evening the needles click, the new and the old weave into a pattern, and there is neither guilt nor greedy hunger in it.

But constant diluting is tiring. Every pleasure comes with inner bargaining: how much is allowed, isn’t it too much, isn’t it time to stop? Strength holds the pull gently, yet it has to hold it all the time, and the Devil’s chain doesn’t disappear — it just becomes familiar. On a tired evening the garland of flowers snaps, the whole basket is paid for, and in the morning the counting starts again. The joy is spent on guarding itself.

svadhisthana:17-18-8.heading: Bringing a hazy image into the light
paragraphs: At the edge of what can be understood, there is always something that won’t leave you in peace. The Moon in the place of desire means dreams, half-shadows, old legends, an image that stays with you all day though you can’t explain it. The Star shows what you do with it: you create openly and generously — you write, draw, compose, and instead of hiding what you’ve made, you give it away. And Justice comes in the feeling afterwards: the satisfaction is real when the hazy thing has found an exact form and every detail is in its place.

In the morning a scrap of a dream remains: a house on the water, someone calling from the far bank. All day the image floats nearby, and in the evening you sit down to write a story — and the fog slowly takes shape: the hero gets a name, the house an address. You post the finished piece for everyone, without waiting for anyone’s verdict. **The hazy becomes yours once you have given it a clear form and let it go out to people.**

The vulnerable point is waiting for a fair response. Having openly given the story away, you expect a response in proportion to what you put in — and there may be none: silence, a couple of likes, a polite “interesting”. Then the Moon paints in the worst: nobody needs it, it’s bad, it was all for nothing. The imagination that fed your creativity starts feeding doubt, and the scales pass a harsh verdict on incomplete evidence. You feel like keeping the next dream to yourself — and the light you used to share slowly dims.

svadhisthana:17-21-11.heading: Everyone together for one party
paragraphs: You want joy to be shared and full. The World sets this desire: you are drawn to gathering different things into one whole — friends from different circles, music, dancing, a long table — and seeing how it all comes together. The Star shows in what you do: you give generously, without keeping count, just as the figure on the card pours water from two jugs. And Strength keeps the feeling afterwards: a host’s nerves — is everyone all right, will there be enough? — you hold gently, never letting them spoil the evening.

A summer evening you’ve put on for your people: colleagues, neighbours, old school friends who have never met each other. You put on music, make introductions, make sure nobody is left standing alone by the wall. By midnight everyone is dancing, including those who “don’t dance”. **Bringing different people together into one whole and giving them a celebration — that is what fills you up.** In that moment you are in your place, as if the whole world had become complete for a minute.

The weak spot is giving until there’s nothing left. The party is for everyone, but you keep almost nothing for yourself: while the guests dance, you top up drinks, clear away, mind the music. Strength helps you keep a brave face, and you gently hide your tiredness, or your hurt at those who didn’t come. You want the whole to be complete — and every absence feels like a gap. The next morning, doing the washing-up, you suddenly realise that the freest person at the party wasn’t you.

svadhisthana:20-15-8.heading: A hobby reborn and a strict reckoning
paragraphs: An old passion of yours may sleep for years and then wake up in a single day. Judgement explains how this looks in action: you answer a sudden call — you hear a song, find some brushes in a drawer — and return to the forgotten as if it had never left. The Devil feeds the desire: the pull that has come back takes hold of you completely and won’t let go. And Justice sums things up in your feelings: afterwards you honestly count what that time cost and whom it took you away from.

Here is an old guitar, turning up in the cupboard under the stairs. You tune it “just for a minute”, and a week later you know fifteen songs, are choosing new strings and sitting up with it until midnight. Your fingers remember — and with them, the person you were when you first played. **A passion of yours doesn’t die; it waits for a call to come back with new fire.** A whole month runs to the rhythm of chords, and the happiness is real and complete.

It’s worse if the returns go round in circles. The pull knows no measure: evenings, weekends, money — everything goes into one thing. Then the scales switch on: so much time, while chores pile up and loved ones miss you. You pass a stern verdict on yourself and put the guitar away again — this time with guilt. The passion falls asleep until the next call, and it all repeats. Each time, the joy is fully resurrected, and then buried again without ever being given a permanent place.

svadhisthana:20-18-11.heading: Where it’s a little bit frightening
paragraphs: You are drawn to places where you can’t see the bottom. The Moon awakens an interest in the unknown, in what both frightens and beckons: improvisation, a forest at night, a stage with no script. Judgement sets the act: when a call sounds inside you, you answer and take the step without waiting for full clarity. And the fear is tamed by Strength: you don’t deny it or run from it, you gently soothe it — and afterwards you are left with a quiet pride.

Your first evening at an improv class: you walk on stage without knowing what you’ll say a second from now, your partner throws you a line — and you have to answer. Your heart pounds, your imagination offers three options at once, you pick one and suddenly hear the audience laugh. **You are drawn to where it’s a little frightening, and that is exactly where life feels sharpest.** After an evening like that, ordinary days feel roomier and your own strength greater.

The trouble is that calm things start to taste bland. If pleasure only comes at the edge, an ordinary walk or a quiet evening with a book leaves you cold, and you go looking again for somewhere more frightening. The Moon paints more promise into the unknown than is really there. And you tame fear so habitually that you stop telling apart when it’s just nerves and when it’s a sensible hint to stop. The courage that once brought joy turns into a compulsory test of yourself.

svadhisthana:14-21-8.heading: Patches sewn into a whole pattern
paragraphs: A patchwork quilt is a good image for your Svadhisthana. Temperance shows in how you spend your time: you enjoy joining different things — fabrics, colours, textures, ideas — matching and mixing until opposites start to get along. And the World draws you on — towards wholeness, towards the moment when scattered pieces come together into one finished cloth. The joy afterwards comes from Justice: it feels good when every piece has its rightful place and nothing outweighs the rest.

You lay the squares out on the floor: bright next to muted, floral beside check. You swap them round, step back, swap them again. For weeks the quilt grows, and then one evening the last seam closes the pattern — and you see the whole thing at once. **Pleasure arrives when scattered parts come together into a whole and no single part is left out.** The quilt goes on the bed, and the whole room seems somehow finished.

What can let you down is the demand for perfect completeness. One square that “upsets the balance” can spoil all the joy: you unpick the seam, choose again, and the finish moves further away. Temperance is ready to look for combinations forever, and the World won’t accept the work as finished until it is flawless. The pleasure of the process gives way to a strict inspection: is everything fair, is everything in place? And a thing that could already be keeping someone warm lies unfinished in the basket.

svadhisthana:17-9-8.heading: Knowledge from silence, given freely
paragraphs: Your interest is born in solitude. It is lit by the Hermit: you want to go deep into a subject, by the light of your own lantern, and work it out yourself — without hurry or other people’s hints. But in what you do, there is the Star: you don’t hide what you’ve found, you give it generously — you tell, show, teach. And satisfaction is measured out by Justice: it comes when the exchange is fair — the knowledge passed on accurately, your contribution noticed and accepted.

Say you have taken up birdwatching. At dawn you are alone on the shore with binoculars: taking notes, checking the field guide, waiting for a rare call. Then you post photos and write for beginners — how to tell a chaffinch from a brambling, where to look for bullfinches in winter. Someone hears a nightingale for the first time thanks to your tip and says thank you. **Knowledge gained in silence becomes joy once you have given it away.** The lantern’s light reaches others.

The vulnerable point is a tally kept without noticing. You give a lot, yet sometimes all that comes back is more requests — “what’s this one?”, “post more” — with no thanks and no interest in how it was gathered. The scales tip, and generosity starts to look naive. Then the Hermit takes over: you close the page, retreat to your birds and share less and less often. The knowledge remains, but the joy of giving, the very thing it grew for, quietly slips away.

svadhisthana:17-12-11.heading: Lying on the water, looking at the sky
paragraphs: You know how to give yourself to pleasure completely, without armour. That is the Star in your actions: openly, generously, without looking back — diving into a lake, bursting into song, dropping everything for a sunset. What draws you most are the Hanged Man’s moments, when time seems to stop and the world appears from the other side. And Strength colours what remains afterwards — a gentle courage: you let yourself trust, and you handled your nerves without crushing them.

Summer, a lake, warm water. You swim out from the shore, turn onto your back and go still: sky above, depth below, and nothing that needs doing. It’s a little frightening — it’s dark beneath you and a long way to the bottom — but you breathe evenly, and the fear recedes. **Trusting the moment completely, without holding on to the shore — that is your pleasure.** You come out of the water as if washed clean inside, with a clear head and a lightness through your whole body.

Only such moments need space, and everyday life doesn’t provide it. The Star generously hands your time to others, the Hanged Man is willing to wait, and Strength gently soothes: “later”. And your own pleasure is left hanging in mid-air: the lake next summer, the song when nobody can hear. Waiting becomes a habit, postponing the norm. You carefully keep the desire safe, yet never let it happen — even though one free evening would be enough for a moment outside of time.

svadhisthana:20-6-8.heading: Calling the old crowd to play again
paragraphs: Perhaps in your circle, you are the one who says: “Shall we do it again?” Judgement in action is the ability to hear a call and raise from oblivion something that seemed over: an old band, hiking trips, board-game nights. The Lovers draw you to it: what matters is not so much the activity as the people you are open with and connected to. And the measure of joy is Justice: it is complete when involvement is mutual and everyone puts their fair share into the common cause.

Suppose a group of friends once had a band of their own, and then life scattered everyone across different cities and schedules. You write in the old group chat, book a rehearsal room for Saturday, and a month later four grown-ups are playing the same songs again, only better. **You know how to revive a shared joy that the others thought was long gone.** Everyone brings something of their own, nobody hogs the spotlight, and the music sounds like a conversation between equals.

It’s harder when you’re the only one who hears the call. The initiative is yours again: you write, remind, book, while someone is late and someone hasn’t learned their part. Justice starts keeping score: who put in effort and who just turned up. The joy of meeting slowly gives way to resentment, and at some point you pass a verdict: “They don’t need this.” The shared project falls asleep again — not because the desire has gone, but because nobody ever talked about give and take out loud.

svadhisthana:20-9-11.heading: A week of quiet to want again
paragraphs: Quiet can give you more than a month of entertainment. The Hermit is the source of desire: interest arises when you are alone with yourself, free of other people’s expectations, and can make out the light of your own lantern. Judgement sets the act: you answer this inner call in earnest — you leave behind what has long stopped bringing joy and take up something new. And Strength works in your feelings: whatever rises up in the quiet — longing, unease, doubt — you don’t drive away but soothe, letting it settle.

You go away for a week to a cabin by a lake — no internet, no plans. The first two days are uncomfortable and your thoughts run in circles, but you don’t escape. On the third you suddenly pick up a pencil you haven’t touched in a long while and draw until dark. **After time alone with yourself, you hear what you truly want — and answer it at once.** You come back with a new passion and a feeling that something inside you has woken up.

The renewal, though, happens alone. The people close to you only see the result: you have dropped your old hobby and are absorbed in something unfamiliar. It’s hard for them to keep up, and hard for you to explain what happened in the quiet. Strength gently soothes even your longing for people, so their absence is barely felt. Each new call leads you further away, and the joy that wakes so brightly in solitude is less and less often shared with anyone.
